s.t: Andy Bell would introduce it: “When I was a little girl, I asked my mummy, ‘Can I be gay when I grow up?’ ‘Yes, if you show a little respect.’”
s.src: Songfacts: A Little Respect (citing Spin, February 1989)
s.q: according to Spin magainze (February 1989), he would sometimes introduce this song on stage by saying: "When I was a little girl, I asked my mummy, 'Can I be gay when I grow up?' She replied, 'Yes if you show a little respect."

s.t: Reviewing Erasure's ‘A Little Respect’ in 1988, NME's Jack Barron called it “Abba with a sex change. Agnetha Faltskog without the beard.”
s.q: Jack Barron from NME said, "In point of fact this is a classic Vince Clarke slice of melodramatic Euro-synth-disco. Hypnotic, splendidly sung, it's Abba with a sex change. Agnetha Faltskog without the beard."

s.t: When Wheatus's 2001 cover outcharted Erasure's original, reaching No. 3, Andy Bell nicknamed them “Weetabix” because he found them “a little weedy”.
s.src: Songfacts: A Little Respect (citing Metro, 22 January 2003)
s.q: Andy Bell said in the Metro newspaper January 22, 2003: "I thought 'A Little Respect' by Wheatus was OK. I call them Weetabix because I find them a little weedy - they're very young."

s.t: Its video, acting out the lyrics literally, was directed by Throbbing Gristle co-founder Peter Christopherson; it's one of the few videos Vince Clarke admits to enjoying making.
s.q: The video showed Clarke and Bell acting out the lyrics literally, sometimes to rather ludicrous effect. It is one of the few videos Vince admits to actually enjoy making.

s.t: After Hull KR fans' singing of Erasure's ‘A Little Respect’ went viral in 2015, Andy Bell let the rugby league club's players record their own charity single of it.
s.q: social media videos of Hull Kingston Rovers supporters singing the song following their semi-final victory against Warrington Wolves went viral, resulting in Andy Bell granting the club's players and staff permission to record a charity single

f.t: As a teenage fan, Andy Bell practised singing along to Vince Clarke's band Yazoo; answering a Melody Maker advert for a singer, he had no idea it was Clarke's.
f.src: Yahoo Entertainment: Erasure's Vince Clarke and Andy Bell talk fateful first audition (2020)
f.q: the teenage Bell was basically a Clarke fanboy who used to practice singing to Yazoo's Upstairs at Eric's and Moyet's solo album Alf ... when he later answered an ad in the Melody Maker that read, "Established songwriter looking for versatile singer," he had no idea that the songwriter in question was his hero.

f.t: Vince Clarke later said he couldn't remember exactly why he left Depeche Mode after their first album, and that he thought he would go back to working for British Rail.
f.q: He later said he couldn't remember exactly why he left, but potentially due to ego problems, thinking he would go back to work for British Rail.

f.t: Their only UK No. 1 was Abba-esque, an EP of ABBA covers in 1992; Andy Bell feels it made people forget that they wrote their own songs.
f.q: When we did the ABBA cover versions thing ['Abba-esque' EP, 1992], which I'm glad we did, but in some ways it kind of dissipated the fact that we were writers.

f.t: Their first album, Wonderland, was a flop, which Andy Bell calls lucky: it left only one hit, ‘Oh L'amour’, to live up to.
f.q: I think we were kind of fortunate because our first album ['Wonderland', 1986] was a flop, so we only had 'Oh L'amour' [as a hit] on that album.

nf.t: NME called it “Abba with a sex change”
nf.q: it's Abba with a sex change.
